intro_script: Welcome to your daily Research News Digest for October 2nd, 2026. We've got deep dives into AI, data infrastructure, and agent capabilities. Today we cover EHR data, local AI assistants, and SLM eligibility.
outro_script: And that's all for your daily dose of research! Dive deep into the world of EHR2Trace. Until tomorrow, keep questioning and exploring! Thanks for tuning in.

items.title: EHR2Trace: Auditable EHR Data Infrastructure for Patient World Models and Clinical Agents
items.summary: EHR2Trace is a system designed to convert Electronic Health Record (EHR) data from various sources into traceable patient events for model training and evaluation. It links these events to their source records and separates event time from information availability, distinguishing between medication orders, dispensing, and administration. The system supports shared event representations compatible with OMOP and MEDS exports, incorporating automated validation. Experiments demonstrated that data structure significantly impacts model performance, with assigning later diagnoses affecting measured accuracy. Ultimately, EHR2Trace provides a reusable data foundation for developing patient world models and clinical agents.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "EHR2Trace: Auditable EHR Data Infrastructure for Patient World Models and Clinical Agents" details a system designed to convert Electronic Health Record data into traceable patient events for model training and evaluation. The research demonstrates that the data structure significantly impacts model performance, with assigning later diagnoses affecting measured accuracy. The EHR2Trace system links EHR events to their source records, separating event time from information availability and distinguishing between medication orders, dispensing, and administration. The system supports shared event representations compatible with OMOP and MEDS exports, incorporating automated validation across various data sources. Experiments revealed that the structure of the data directly influences the resulting model accuracy. This work establishes a reusable data foundation for developing patient world models and clinical agents. Future developments will focus on the application of this infrastructure in clinical AI systems.

items.title: K-Dense BYOK: An Open-Source AI Research Assistant That Runs Locally and Keeps a Hash-Chained Lab Notebook
items.summary: K-Dense BYOK is a free, open-source AI research assistant designed for scientists that runs directly on the researcher's local computer. It allows users to leverage any chosen model while providing scientific scaffolding, workflow templates, and a complete, hash-chained lab notebook. The system records agent actions rather than relying solely on its output to combat model overclaiming. It guides research through written procedures and roles, tracking all work in a verifiable, immutable record. This tool demonstrated strong performance in research execution and quality across various prompts.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "K-Dense BYOK: An Open-Source AI Research Assistant That Runs Locally and Keeps a Hash-Chained Lab Notebook". This story details an open-source AI research assistant designed for scientists that runs locally and maintains a hash-chained lab notebook. The system demonstrated strong performance in research execution and quality across various prompts. The K-Dense BYOK system functions as a free, open-source assistant enabling users to utilize any chosen model while providing scientific scaffolding and workflow templates. The methodology involves recording agent actions rather than relying solely on model output to mitigate overclaiming, guiding research through written procedures and defined roles. This process tracks all work in a verifiable and immutable record within the lab notebook. The verifiable record ensures that the research execution maintains integrity through the documented steps taken. This advancement suggests a pathway for verifiable and trustworthy execution within local, autonomous AI research environments.

items.title: Measuring the Microtask Eligibility Gap: When Is an Off-the-Shelf SLM Enough for an Agent Harness?
items.summary: Agent harnesses often require small language models (SLMs) for microtasks like command approval and tool selection. A benchmark was created to measure if off-the-shelf SLMs meet practitioner-defined thresholds, which are anchored to a non-LLM baseline. The study found an "eligibility gap" where most configurations failed to meet these thresholds across various models. Quantization to 4-bit did not substantially change this gap, suggesting the issue tracks model size rather than mere precision. The practical implication is to use SLMs only when a performance deficit compared to a baseline is observed.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Measuring the Microtask Eligibility Gap: When Is an Off-the-Shelf SLM Enough for an Agent Harness?" reports on an investigation into the sufficiency of off-the-shelf small language models for agent harnesses. The study found an eligibility gap where most configurations failed to meet practitioner-defined performance thresholds when compared to a non-language model baseline. Researchers established a benchmark to assess whether these models could adequately handle microtasks like command approval and tool selection required by agent systems. The methodology involved testing various model configurations against these established practitioner thresholds. The results indicated that quantization to four-bit precision did not significantly alter this gap, suggesting the performance deficit correlates primarily with the overall model size rather than the level of precision. This implies that small language models should be utilized only when a measurable performance deficit against a baseline is identified. The findings suggest a need for stricter performance validation before deploying off-the-shelf SLMs in complex agent applications.

items.title: From Proposal to Verified Effect: Praxa, an Evidence-Bound Harness for Governed AI Agent Execution
items.summary: Praxa is an agent harness designed to explicitly represent the states of proposal, authority, dispatch, and verified external effect in AI agent execution. It introduces mechanisms for deterministic admission, brokered execution, external read-back, reconciliation, and reviewed promotion. The research presents four evidence lanes, including repository audits, pilot testing, and comparative development analyses. While demonstrating an evidence-bound architecture for making authority-to-effect transitions testable, the current evidence does not establish superiority in security, safety, or performance metrics. Ultimately, Praxa's contribution is an explicit and testable framework rather than a proven lift in autonomous capability.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "From Proposal to Verified Effect: Praxa, an Evidence-Bound Harness for Governed AI Agent Execution" details an agent harness designed to explicitly represent the states of proposal, authority, dispatch, and verified external effect in AI agent execution, presenting an evidence-bound architecture for making authority-to-effect transitions testable. The research introduces mechanisms for deterministic admission, brokered execution, external read-back, reconciliation, and reviewed promotion, supported by four evidence lanes including repository audits, pilot testing, and comparative development analyses. The work demonstrates a framework for governing AI agent execution through a testable structure, though the current evidence does not establish superiority in security, safety, or performance metrics. This contribution establishes an explicit and testable framework for managing agent execution flows within the evolving field of autonomous systems.

items.title: What Do Rationales Communicate? A Message-Intervention Study in Role-Specialized QA
items.summary: Role-specialized QA pipelines pass rationales between reasoners and verifiers, but the effect is unclear regarding answer accuracy or support assessment. A message-intervention diagnostic showed that adding faithful rationales adds little to answer accuracy, but corrupted rationales significantly alter support judgments. Corrupted rationales strongly shift support judgments, and human audits reveal that models often accept corrupted rationales. The study concludes that rationale sharing should be evaluated as a verification-message mechanism rather than solely as a route to better answers.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "What Do Rationales Communicate? A Message-Intervention Study in Role-Specialized QA" investigates the communicative function of rationales within role-specialized question answering pipelines and reveals that the quality of shared rationales significantly impacts support assessments rather than direct answer accuracy. The study employed a message-intervention diagnostic to examine the effect of passing rationales between reasoners and verifiers. The methodology involved manipulating these shared rationales to determine their role in the downstream verification process. The findings indicated that incorporating faithful rationales did not substantially improve answer accuracy, but introducing corrupted rationales resulted in significant shifts in support judgments, as human audits confirmed that models frequently accepted these corrupted rationales. The research concludes that rationale sharing should be evaluated as a verification-message mechanism rather than solely as a pathway to enhanced answers. This suggests that the focus for rationale systems should shift towards robust verification signaling.

items.title: Comedic Fool's Gold: Reward Exploits and Countermeasures in Conversational Humor
items.summary: The research investigates reward exploits and countermeasures in training language models for conversational humor. Two methods are explored to capture understandable surprise and predicted audience amusement, testing how models react to word-shuffled replies. A fluency filter attempts to detect these shuffles, but the combined reward system still allows some exploits. Normalizing laughter cues across speakers blocks some attacks, though unmatched expressions remain exploitable. The study concludes that countermeasures must block exploitable shortcuts while maintaining the intended behavior of the reward.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Comedic Fool's Gold: Reward Exploits and Countermeasures in Conversational Humor" investigates reward exploits and countermeasures in training language models for conversational humor, finding that while some defense mechanisms exist, certain exploitable shortcuts remain. The research explored two methods to capture understandable surprise and predicted audience amusement by testing how models reacted to word-shuffled replies. A fluency filter was introduced to detect these word shuffles, but the combined reward system still permitted certain exploits. Furthermore, normalizing laughter cues across different speakers successfully blocked some of these attacks, though unmatched expressions remained exploitable. The study concluded that countermeasures must successfully block exploitable shortcuts while preserving the intended behavior of the reward system. This research indicates that future development in conversational humor AI requires robust defenses against subtle reward manipulation techniques.

items.title: Block Optimism for Nonstationary Bandits with Latent Linear Dynamics
items.summary: The study addresses a nonstationary stochastic bandit problem featuring latent linear dynamics where actions influence future state evolution and rewards are bilinear in the action and state. Previous methods achieve $\tilde{O}(T^{2/3})$ regret, but the authors propose an adaptive block-level optimism strategy. This involves approximating the infinite-memory reward process with a finite-memory proxy to facilitate planning. A UCB-based block algorithm is introduced to select blocks optimistically based on confidence sets for the truncated dynamics parameters. This approach yields a superior regret bound of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ for this class of problems.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - stat.ML, "Block Optimism for Nonstationary Bandits with Latent Linear Dynamics" addresses a nonstationary stochastic bandit problem with latent linear dynamics, proposing an adaptive block-level optimism strategy that achieves a superior regret bound of approximately the square root of the time horizon. The research introduces an approach to approximate the infinite-memory reward process using a finite-memory proxy to enable planning in the context where actions influence future state evolution and rewards exhibit bilinear dependence on action and state. A UCB-based block algorithm is implemented to select blocks optimistically based on confidence sets derived from the truncated dynamics parameters, resulting in a regret bound of order $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$. This methodology successfully navigates the complexities of nonstationary environments with latent dynamics. The findings indicate a more efficient planning strategy for decision-making in dynamic and evolving systems.

items.title: Scientific Agents: Evaluating Profession-Specific System Prompts on Scientific Tasks
items.summary: Profession-specific system prompts increase token usage and cost without providing a consistent accuracy improvement for scientific tasks. Evaluation of Scientific Agents showed no statistically clear accuracy gain from using these detailed profiles over baseline settings. Matched profiles resulted in significantly higher token usage and cost per successful call to the model. While longer prompts offered a minor advantage in specific error scenarios, this was attributed more to prompt length than domain expertise. Loading full profession profiles by default did not improve accuracy or cost considerably.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Scientific Agents: Evaluating Profession-Specific System Prompts on Scientific Tasks" details an evaluation of profession-specific system prompts on scientific tasks, finding that these prompts do not yield a consistent accuracy improvement and result in increased token usage and cost. The study evaluated scientific agents by comparing performance using detailed, profession-specific profiles against baseline settings. The research assessed whether incorporating detailed profiles enhanced accuracy for scientific tasks, observing that there was no statistically clear accuracy gain from these profiles. Matched profiles demonstrated significantly higher token usage and cost per successful model call. While longer prompts provided a minor advantage in specific error scenarios, this improvement was attributed more to prompt length than actual domain expertise. Loading full profession profiles by default did not result in a substantial improvement in either accuracy or cost. This research suggests that extensive domain-specific prompting may not be the most efficient method for improving performance in scientific agent applications.

items.title: Characterizing a Configuration Where Inference-Time PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting Is Inert: Evidence from Three Reasoning LMs
items.summary: The study investigates the effectiveness of inference-time PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting (PPFG) for transferring knowledge in reasoning Language Models. The research tests PPFG on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Math-Shepherd across multiple benchmarks and models. Results indicate that PPFG is statistically indistinguishable from an independent parallel Chain-of-Thought baseline in stagnation and random-targeting scenarios. The analysis reveals that injected grafts often target chains that were already successful or near completion, suggesting the mechanism is not heuristic-specific. The work contributes an equivalence-testing template to establish nulls for inference-time mechanism effects.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Characterizing a Configuration Where Inference-Time PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting Is Inert: Evidence from Three Reasoning LMs" investigates the effectiveness of inference-time PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting for knowledge transfer in reasoning Language Models, finding that the method is statistically indistinguishable from an independent parallel Chain-of-Thought baseline in stagnation and random-targeting scenarios. The research examined the application of PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting on the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model utilizing the Math-Shepherd method across several benchmarks and models. The analysis demonstrated that the injected grafts frequently targeted chains that were already successful or nearing completion, indicating that the mechanism observed is not dependent on heuristic-specific targeting. This work establishes an equivalence-testing template for null results concerning inference-time mechanism effects. The findings provide a benchmark for understanding the efficacy of knowledge grafting techniques in complex reasoning systems.

items.title: Gradient-Aligned Pair Selection for Personalized Preference Optimization
items.summary: Personalizing large language models requires selecting preference pairs based on user preferences rather than aggregate quality. Existing methods use heuristics for pair selection, which can degrade personalization. The research frames personalized preference learning as a geometry-aligned optimization problem by examining gradient interactions. This insight suggests that pair selection is a geometric decision influencing personalization advancement. The proposed GAP-DPO algorithm uses utility-aware, geometry-aligned selection to improve stylistic fidelity and generation quality.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Gradient-Aligned Pair Selection for Personalized Preference Optimization" reports on a method for selecting preference pairs in large language model fine-tuning based on individual user preferences. This research frames personalized preference learning as a geometry-aligned optimization problem by examining gradient interactions, suggesting that pair selection is a geometric decision influencing personalization advancement. The proposed GAP-DPO algorithm employs utility-aware, geometry-aligned selection to improve both stylistic fidelity and generation quality by focusing on gradient alignments. This methodology moves beyond heuristic pair selection by analyzing the geometric relationship between preferences and model updates to achieve better personalization. This work indicates a new direction for optimizing large language models through geometrically informed selection processes.

items.title: Heavy-Tailed Memory Traces in Long-Horizon Language Agents
items.summary: Long-horizon language agents use external memory where memory use exhibits heavy-tailed traces, concentrating on a core while rare states accumulate prediction errors. This effect is reproducible and depends on the agent's policy, with semantic LLM policies yielding the strongest truncated-power-law-compatible traces. The authors propose the Core--Tail World Model (CTWM), a rank-based memory controller to manage prompt budget effectively. Applying CTWM reduces prompt tokens and lowers prediction errors relative to baseline memory methods on synthetic graph worlds. These findings suggest heavy-tailed memory traces serve as a practical control signal for token-efficient agent world models.

items.title: Hermes: Learning Contextual Reasoning Unlocks Test-Time Scaling
items.summary: Test-time scaling requires effectively managing context allocation and reuse across multiple context windows during inference. The authors introduce Hermes, a family of harnesses, and Hermes-Learn, a two-stage framework, to enable models to make these allocation decisions. Capable models can utilize this flexibility to scale with extra compute, whereas smaller models struggle without training with Hermes-Learn. This training induces adaptive contextual reasoning strategies that generalize across benchmarks and transfer to other scaling methods. Ultimately, learning contextual reasoning unlocks the ability to scale model performance during inference.

items.title: Travel Time Prediction in Supply Chain Management Using Machine Learning
items.summary: Research uses machine learning and deep learning to accurately predict travel times within supply chain transportation and logistics. Accurate travel time estimation is vital for improving logistics consistency, demand forecasting, lead time management, and assembly planning. The study leverages large historical data and novel techniques to build an accurate model for predicting inventory travel times. This prediction is crucial for supply chain members to enhance delivery performance and ultimately improve customer satisfaction.

items.title: Inference for stochastic differential equations driven by weighted sub-fractional Brownian motion using neural networks and the Euler approximation
items.summary: The research focuses on inferring parameters of stochastic differential equations driven by weighted sub-fractional Brownian motion using neural networks and the Euler approximation. The framework considers an SDE driven by a Gaussian process with a specific covariance structure related to a temporal weight function. The method uses the Euler approximation to reconstruct Gaussian driving increments and estimate a trajectory likelihood. Neural and radial-basis representations are employed to model the drift, diffusion, and temporal weight. The approach compares its performance against other neural methods for parameter estimation.

items.title: Conformal Adversarial Generative Ensemble
items.summary: The Conformal Adversarial Generative Ensemble (CAGE) is a novel framework designed to improve time series forecasting by mitigating the influence of extreme forecasts. It integrates generative modeling, adversarial discrimination, and conformal prediction to enhance forecast reliability. CAGE uses multiple generative models to create initial forecasts, which are then assessed by a discriminative component employing conformal prediction. P-values from nonconformity scores dynamically adjust model weights, ensuring only credible predictions influence the final ensemble output. Empirical results on milk collection and public health data show CAGE outperforms traditional ensembles in handling noise and outliers.

items.title: A Data-Free Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Level-Set Interface Advection
items.summary: A data-free physics-informed neural operator is developed for level-set interface advection. This operator maps an initial interface to its full spatiotemporal trajectory under a prescribed flow. Training relies solely on the transport residual and a geometric constraint, without using any reference solutions. The method demonstrates significant performance gains over supervised baselines, achieving error reductions of a factor of 4.4 for a single vortex. The physics-trained operator conserves enclosed area better than the supervised baseline in certain conditions.

items.title: Fractional Laplace Neural Operators: Exact Architectures, an Expressivity Frontier at Criticality, and Certified Stability for Memory-Driven Network Dynamics
items.summary: Fractional Laplace neural operators (fLNOs) are introduced to embed the memory structure found in hereditary network dynamics, which are described by Volterra resolvents. For commuting excitation-Laplacian pairs, a block graph-spectral layer exactly represents the linear Volterra solution operator. The expressivity frontier shows that finite rational realizations approximate fractional memory geometrically but cannot capture non-integer critical asymptotics. The framework allows for trainable parametrizations that enforce stability margins and separate genuine operator consistency from parameter sharing.

items.title: Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Image Regression Models with Application to an Inertial Confinement Fusion Emulator
items.summary: Uncertainty quantification is necessary for black-box image regression models in high-stakes applications. Adaptive Conformal Prediction using Nearest Neighbors (ACPNN) is proposed as an input-adaptive conformal framework for image regression. ACPNN generates locally adaptive uncertainty estimates by leveraging neighboring samples defined by a Gaussian Process with an ARD kernel. The method is computationally efficient while maintaining reliable uncertainty quantification. This approach was demonstrated effectively on a diffusion model emulating inertial confinement fusion simulations.

items.title: ChainLoRA: Geometry-Preserving Task Vector Merging for Continual Learning in LLMs
items.summary: ChainLoRA is a replay-free continual learning framework designed for large language models by merging task vectors in a geometry-preserving manner. It formulates forgetting through a geometric view of task updates, separating directional overlap from coefficient coupling. The method combines chain-updated training with post-stream adaptive SVD merging for parameter integration. Procrustes adaptation aligns a shared carrier to the latest task, facilitating the geometric separation of task-specific components. Experiments demonstrate that ChainLoRA achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks while managing parameter budgets effectively.

items.title: Weighted Data Selection: Sharp Upper-Half and Five-Dimensional Laws
items.summary: The paper investigates the risk retained by a small reweighted training set in finite weighted least squares with a minimum-norm learner. It proves the exact law $\Gamma_d(n)=3-n/d$ for the specific range $\lceil3d/2\rceil\leq n\leq2d-1$. The guarantee is achieved by using selections that preserve the full feature span, employing balanced simplex anchors, and methods like positive-weight lifting. For a specific small budget $(d,n)=(5,6)$, the bound $\Gamma_5(6)=11/5$ is matched, with a sharpness of $6/5$ verified using circuit-based and geometric methods.

items.title: Activation-Conditioned Self-Distillation
items.summary: Activation-Conditioned Self-Distillation (ACSD) extracts a steering vector by contrasting activations of self-generated trajectories leading to correct answers against other trajectories. A frozen base model applies this vector to predict the next token based on student-generated prefixes. The student learns from the next-token distributions of these prefixes, utilizing outcome verification for direction construction and calibration. Distillation is performed without needing problem-specific reference text or teacher parameter updates. ACSD achieves the highest mean accuracy across four mathematical benchmarks among evaluated methods.

items.title: FlashDiffusion: Fused Tiled Kernel Spectral Decomposition
items.summary: Diffusion maps and kernel methods offer an interpretable spectral representation for geometric learning. Dense Gaussian kernel methods require $O(N^2)$ memory, which is prohibitive for high-rank matrices. FlashDiffusion is a matrix-free method that evaluates dense Gaussian kernel blocks using fused GPU tiles. It couples the eigensolver with an empirical $\beta$-flow to select the finite-sample resolution scale. This approach warm-starts expensive spectral solves by continuing over coarser resolutions.

items.title: DualCast: A Dual-Path Language Model for Bimodal Financial Time-Series Forecasting
items.summary: DualCast is a dual-path language model framework designed for bimodal financial time-series forecasting. It utilizes a frozen language model augmented with a discrete financial vocabulary, representing log-return patches with summary tokens. A fast path trains embeddings on a frozen backbone, while a slow path uses a toggleable LoRA adapter to condition on external news for revised predictions. The slow path, optimized with a return-space group policy, achieved the lowest mean absolute percentage error in several evaluations. This approach effectively combines a fast numerical forecaster with an optional text-conditioned revision mechanism.

items.title: Transferable Graph Metanetworks
items.summary: Weight space networks predict properties of neural networks by taking another network's weights as input. Prior work struggled with generalizing performance to networks of different sizes. Transferable Graph Metanetworks modify the model to improve performance transfer across networks of varying widths. The modifications are based on invariance and continuity principles for function representation. Empirical results show significant size generalization, especially when training under maximal-update parameterization, supported by infinite-width limit theory.

items.title: Target-Dependent Limits of Causal Repair: A Leading-Log Frontier in a Gaussian Model
items.summary: The research quantifies the gap between how much a causal predictor can improve and the gain actually learned during a causal repair in a Gaussian model. It uses auxiliary data to estimate effect magnitudes up to bounded contamination and diagnostics to identify direction in a causal experiment. Joint optimization of the learner and assessor under a uniform learning MSE helps avoid trivial solutions, showing a $k^{-2}$ assessment floor at the usual learning scale. A leading-log frontier is characterized by an assessment exponent of $\min{\ell_k,2k\eta_k/U}$ in the magnitude-rich regime. This work specifies how the assessment target influences information requirements in causal experiments.

items.title: Kinematic signatures of impairment: Detecting alcohol intoxication in e-scooter riders using sensor data and machine learning
items.summary: Alcohol intoxication is a risk factor for e-scooter crashes, necessitating real-time impairment detection. Researchers used sensor data from an instrumented e-scooter and a six-axis IMU to study kinematic signatures of impairment. Analysis of normalized permutation entropy and standard deviation revealed that intoxicated riders exhibit reduced temporal complexity and increased signal amplitude compared to sober riders. A machine learning classifier achieved 85% accuracy in distinguishing between sober and intoxicated states based on these kinematic features. This work establishes a method using onboard sensing and entropy analysis for automatic intoxication detection in e-scooter riders.

items.title: Learning to Price Electricity for Optimal Demand Response
items.summary: A neural-network-based algorithm is proposed for contextual energy pricing to optimize demand response. This method models pricing as a Stackelberg game and uses a mean-field solution representation. The algorithm learns constrained mappings from contextual features, such as weather and time patterns, to feasible price signals. Simulations across US cities demonstrate that incorporating this contextual information significantly increases the value of demand response programs.

items.title: A Moving-Horizon Approximate Branch-and-Reduce Method for Deep Classification Trees
items.summary: The method proposes a moving-horizon approximate branch-and-reduce approach for training deep classification trees on large datasets with continuous features. It leverages a hierarchical root-subtree optimization framework, using branch-and-reduce for the root and greedy heuristics for subtree approximation. This approximation acts as a lookahead rollout, enhancing efficiency for deeper structures, and a low-cost strategy refines model accuracy iteratively. Numerical results show the method surpasses heuristic baselines in accuracy while offering superior scalability concerning dataset size and tree depth.

items.title: When Do Causal World Models Help Modular LLM Agents
items.summary: Causal world models are studied for modular LLM agents where actions in one module affect others. The research introduces FedCausalCompose, a framework using causal world-models to provide intervention-response evidence for cross-module interfaces. Causal interfaces prove most beneficial in structured tool environments where API signatures reveal preconditions and effects. However, this benefit is less pronounced in dialogue and narrative settings unless causal information is explicitly made relevant at action time. Therefore, causal world models are most helpful when cross-module interfaces are statistically identifiable and presented in an actionable format.
